html:
Tonkin is the old European name for northern Vietnam, the land around the Red River Delta and Hanoi. From 1883 to early 1945 it was a French protectorate inside French Indochina. The map shows it in 1945, the year French rule there broke down.

In the 1600s and 1700s the name meant the realm of the Trịnh lords, who ruled the north in the name of the Lê emperors. France took it in the 1880s after wars with the Black Flags and Qing China. Under French rule coal mines and railways served French interests.

1945 was a year of upheaval:

  • In March the Japanese, who had kept troops in Indochina since 1940, overthrew the French administration and set up a nominally independent Vietnam under the emperor Bảo Đại.
  • The famine of 1944 and 1945 killed a vast number of people in the north, often put at a million or more.
  • After Japan surrendered in August, the Viet Minh took power in the August Revolution, and on 2 September Ho Chi Minh declared the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi.

France returned in 1946, and the First Indochina War followed.
